analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly workers a right to request schedule changes without retaliation and requires two weeks' notice, with extra pay for last-minute changes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given workers at companies with 15 or more employees the right to ask for changes to their hours, shift times, or work location without being fired or punished for asking [S2]. Employers would have to discuss the request in good faith and grant it for caregiving, health, school, or second-job reasons unless they had a specific business reason not to [S2]. Workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses would get their schedules at least 14 days in advance, extra pay when employers change shifts late or cancel them, and extra pay for split shifts and short rests between shifts [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses — the occupations where the bill's findings say unpredictable scheduling is most common. The bill's own findings cite survey data that about two-thirds of hourly retail and food service workers get less than two weeks' notice of their schedules, and 65 percent want a more stable schedule [S2]. Workers juggling child care, health care, school, or a second job would gain the most, since employers could only refuse those requests for a defined business reason [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food service, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Workers could request changes to hours, shift times, work location, or advance notice, and the employer must engage in a good-faith interactive process and give written reasons for any denial [S2].

For requests tied to a serious health condition, caregiving, education or training, or a second job, the employer must grant the request unless it has a bona fide business reason — a defined list including significant cost, inability to meet customer demand, or insufficient work [S2].
Covered sector employees would get schedules at least 14 days ahead, with $75 per day compensation when notice is not given, plus an annual written estimate of their minimum monthly hours [S2].

Last-minute schedule changes would trigger predictability pay: an extra hour of pay when hours are added or shifted, and at least half-time pay for scheduled hours the employer cancels; split shifts earn one extra hour of pay [S2].
Workers could decline shifts starting less than 11 hours after a previous shift without penalty, or accept them at 1.5 times pay — directly targeting the 'clopening' shifts the bill describes [S2].

Retaliation for exercising these rights — firing, demotion, cutting hours — would be unlawful, with employees able to sue for lost wages, doubled liquidated damages, and attorney's fees, and the Labor Department empowered to investigate and fine violators [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large retail chains, restaurants, hotels, cleaning companies, and warehouse operators — the employers whose scheduling practices the bill regulates. They would bear the cost of 14-day advance scheduling, predictability and split-shift pay, penalties of $75 per day for missing notice deadlines, and potential civil fines and private lawsuits [S2]. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through scheduling software and administrative changes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on employers, who must pay premiums for schedule changes, cancellations, and split shifts, and could face $75-per-day penalties for missed notice deadlines — costs that small businesses and thin-margin restaurants argue are hard to absorb [S2].

The bill requires a 14-day posted schedule and written consent for off-schedule hours, which could make it harder for employers to respond to genuine surges in customer demand or unexpected staff absences without paying premiums [S2].

The good-faith interactive process and written-denial requirements add administrative recordkeeping for every schedule request, and enforcement through employee lawsuits with doubled damages creates litigation exposure even for employers acting in good faith, though courts can waive doubled damages for good-faith violations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for workers — predictable schedules that make child care, second jobs, and schooling feasible — are substantial and well documented in the bill's own findings, and the bill cites employer pilot data (a Gap Inc. pilot showed higher sales and productivity with stable scheduling) suggesting the costs are manageable [S2]. The real costs are compliance and scheduling flexibility for employers in low-margin industries, and some risk of litigation. The tradeoff is real but modest compared with the instability the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Schedules That Work Act on September 19, 2023, joined by 19 Democratic senators and one Independent [S1][S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S4].
No House companion action is recorded in the bill's history; the bill's only actions are its introduction and committee referral [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, cleaning, and warehouse employers are better off: they never had to comply with 14-day scheduling notice, predictability pay, or split-shift premiums, and avoided the associated compliance costs and litigation exposure. Workers with unstable schedules got no relief.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 19 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who chaired the committee it was referred to.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and no floor vote was ever scheduled in the chamber they could have blocked with the 60-vote threshold.

against.name: Retail, restaurant, and hospitality industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of predictive-scheduling mandates, which they argue raise labor costs and reduce flexibility in low-margin industries.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond a Democratic-chaired committee.

industries.note: Retail sales and cashier occupations are covered by the 14-day notice, predictability pay, and split-shift pay requirements, and employers face $75-per-day penalties for missed notice. The industry's scheduling flexibility — the 'just-in-time' practices the bill targets — is the cost savings the bill would remove.

Food preparation and serving occupations are covered sector employees subject to advance notice, predictability pay, and rest requirements. The industry's cost is workers' schedule stability; the bill cites data that two-thirds of these workers get less than two weeks' notice.

Hospitality establishment employees are explicitly covered, facing the same notice and pay-premium mandates. Hotels relying on on-call and clopening scheduling would bear the compliance and premium costs.
Warehouse establishment employees are covered by the scheduling requirements, which would constrain the volatile scheduling practices the bill's findings say are common in these occupations.
Cleaning occupations are covered sector employees subject to the advance notice and pay-premium requirements.
